title: Word order and nominal clauses

objectives.can: Find subject, verb and object in an Aramaic clause whatever their order, and read clauses with no verb or with אִיתַי.

explanation.summary: Biblical Aramaic does not keep to one fixed order of subject, verb and object, and many clauses have no verb at all. You find the parts of a clause by their forms (the verb's ending, a prefixed לְ, the pronoun that links two nouns), not by their position.

sections.heading: Several orders are normal
body: Look first at a plain narrative clause. In Daniel 3:1 the order is the one English has: נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּר מַלְכָּא עֲבַד צְלֵם, 'King Nebuchadnezzar made an image'. Subject, then verb, then object.

But the verb does not have to stay in the middle. In Ezra 6:13 the subject stands first, a long clause about what Darius had sent comes next, and the main verb עֲבַדוּ is the very last word of the sentence. In Daniel 6:8 the opposite happens: the verb אִתְיָעַטוּ comes first and its subject, 'all the officials of the kingdom', follows. In Daniel 2:19 a phrase of place comes first, then the subject רָזָה, and the verb גֲלִי ('was revealed') ends the clause.

Grammarians often note that, compared with Hebrew narrative, the verb comes later in Aramaic and the object may stand before it, above all in Ezra's official letters and in Daniel. The usual scholarly explanation is the influence of Akkadian and of the Persian administration, whose documents put the verb late. That is an explanation of where the habit came from, not a rule you can use to read a clause: each clause has to be read from its forms.

sections.heading: How to find subject, verb and object
body: Start with the verb. Its ending tells you who or what acts: the ending of שָׂמְתָּ in Daniel 3:10 is 'you' (masculine singular), and that of כְּתַבוּ in Ezra 4:8 is 'they'. A noun or pronoun that agrees with the ending is the subject, wherever it stands. An independent pronoun such as אַנְתְּ in Daniel 3:10 is not needed for the sense, so it adds stress or points at the person addressed.

Next look for the object. An object may follow the verb (אִגְּרָה, 'a letter', in Ezra 4:8) or come before it. In Daniel 3:12 the clause לֵאלָהָךְ לָא פָלְחִין means 'your god they do not serve': the object לֵאלָהָךְ stands first, before the negative and the participle, and its prefix לְ marks it as the object (the לְ of the previous lessons). A word with another preposition, such as עַל or מִן, is not an object.

Then check what is left. Phrases of time or place (בֵּהּ בְּלֵילְיָא, 'in that night', Daniel 5:30) may open a clause. They are not the subject. In Daniel 5:30 the order is time phrase, verb (קְטִיל), then subject: בֵּלְאשַׁצַּר מַלְכָּא.

sections.heading: Clauses with no verb
body: Aramaic has no word for 'is' that must appear. A clause may simply put two parts side by side, the thing spoken about and what is said of it. This is called a nominal clause.

Very often a pronoun stands between the two parts, linking them. In Daniel 2:38 Daniel tells the king אַנְתְּה הוּא רֵאשָׁה דִּי דַהֲבָא: 'you are the head of gold'. In Daniel 2:47 the king says אֱלָהֲכוֹן הוּא אֱלָהּ אֱלָהִין, 'your God is the God of gods'. In clauses like these הוּא is not a second subject. It is a pronoun that marks the join between subject and predicate (grammarians call it a pronoun used as a copula). The same word can also be an ordinary subject, as in Daniel 2:22, where הוּא begins a clause about what God reveals: a nominal clause has a noun or pronoun before it, a verbal clause has a verb after it.

Possession is also said without a verb. In Daniel 7:6 the third animal is described with וְלַהּ גַּפִּין אַרְבַּע: literally 'and to it four wings', that is, 'and it had four wings'. In Daniel 7:7 the same pattern ends the verse: וְקַרְנַיִן עֲשַׂר לַהּ, 'ten horns it had'. English needs 'has' or 'had'; Aramaic puts the owner after לְ.

sections.heading: אִיתַי and לָא אִיתַי
body: You met אִיתַי as 'there is'. It states that something exists, and what exists follows: אִיתַי גְּבַר בְּמַלְכוּתָךְ, 'there is a man in your kingdom' (Daniel 5:11). Its negative is לָא אִיתַי, 'there is not': חֲבָל לָא אִיתַי בְּהוֹן in Daniel 3:25 is 'and no hurt is in them', that is, 'they have no hurt'. In Ezra 4:16 חֲלָק ... לָא אִיתַי לָךְ is 'you will have no share' (literally, 'a share is not to you').

אִיתַי can take a pronoun ending and then it stands for a person who 'is' or 'is not' doing something. In Daniel 3:14 the king's question ends לֵאלָהַי לָא אִיתֵיכוֹן פָּלְחִין: 'my god you are not serving'. The ending -כוֹן is 'you' (plural); פָּלְחִין is a participle. The same clause in 3:12 has no אִיתַי (לֵאלָהָךְ לָא פָלְחִין), and the sense is the same. אִיתַי adds emphasis that the thing really is or is not so.

misunderstandings: The first noun is not always the subject. Daniel 2:19 opens with לְדָנִיֵּאל, 'to Daniel', and the subject is רָזָה, 'the mystery'. Read the verb's ending and its meaning first.
An object that stands before the verb is not a subject. In Daniel 3:12 the first words, לֵאלָהָךְ לָא פָלְחִין, mean 'your god they do not serve'; the servants are in the verb's ending.
הוּא does not always mean 'he'. Between two nouns or between a pronoun and a noun it is usually the link of a nominal clause, as in אַנְתְּה הוּא רֵאשָׁה.
A clause with no verb is not unfinished. If you feel that 'is' is missing, add it in English and keep it out of your analysis.

deeper.heading: Why Aramaic put the verb late
body: The Aramaic of Ezra's letters is the language of the Persian chancery, and the Aramaic of Daniel stands in the same wider tradition. Grammarians who compare it with Akkadian, in which the verb comes at the end of the clause, and with the administrative language of Persia suggest that this contact made the late verb and the early object common. Others stress that older Aramaic documents already show free order, so the contact may only have strengthened a habit that was already there. Either way, treat the explanation as background and the clause itself as the evidence.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Nebuchadnezzar the king made an image of gold, whose height was threescore cubits, and the breadth thereof six cubits; he set it up in the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Subject (נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּר מַלְכָּא), verb (עֲבַד), object (צְלֵם): the order English has. The verb's ending is 'he'.

quoted.title: Ezra
quoted.english: Then Tattenai, the governor beyond the River, Shethar-bozenai, and their companions, because that Darius the king had thus sent, acted with all diligence.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The subject, Tattenai the governor with his colleagues, stands near the start. A clause about Darius's sending (שְׁלַח, with its own subject) comes between, and the main verb עֲבַדוּ, 'they did', is the last word.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: and wheresoever the children of men, the beasts of the field, and the fowls of the heaven dwell, hath He given them into thy hand, and hath made thee to rule over them all; thou art the head of gold.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: A nominal clause. אַנְתְּה is the subject, הוּא links it to the predicate, and רֵאשָׁה, 'the head', is the predicate. There is no verb: 'you are the head of gold'.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: there is a man in thy kingdom, in whom is the spirit of the holy gods; and in the days of thy father light and understanding and wisdom, like the wisdom of the gods, was found in him; and the king Nebuchadnezzar thy father, the king, I say, thy father, made him master of the magicians, enchanters, Chaldeans, and astrologers;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: אִיתַי states that something exists. What exists, גְּבַר, 'a man', follows, and בְּמַלְכוּתָךְ says where: 'there is a man in your kingdom'.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: After this I beheld, and lo another, like a leopard, which had upon the sides of it four wings of a fowl; the beast had also four heads; and dominion was given to it.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: A verbless clause of possession. לַהּ, 'to it', comes first and the thing owned, גַּפִּין אַרְבַּע, 'four wings', follows: 'and it had four wings'.

practice.prompt: In נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּר מַלְכָּא עֲבַד צְלֵם (words 0 to 3), in what order do the parts stand?

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Nebuchadnezzar the king made an image of gold, whose height was threescore cubits, and the breadth thereof six cubits; he set it up in the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

practice.explain: נְבוּכַדְנֶצַּר מַלְכָּא is the subject, עֲבַד the verb and צְלֵם the object. This is the order English uses, and it is only one of the orders Aramaic allows.

practice.prompt: Which word is the subject of גֲלִי, 'was revealed' (word 6)?

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Then was the secret revealed unto Daniel in a vision of the night. Then Daniel blessed the God of heaven.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

practice.explain: גֲלִי is passive, so the thing revealed is the subject: the mystery. לְדָנִיֵּאל, 'to Daniel', stands first but is only the person to whom it was revealed.

practice.prompt: What does הוּא (word 14) do in אַנְתְּה הוּא רֵאשָׁה דִּי דַהֲבָא?

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: and wheresoever the children of men, the beasts of the field, and the fowls of the heaven dwell, hath He given them into thy hand, and hath made thee to rule over them all; thou art the head of gold.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It links the subject to the predicate, like English 'are'
practice.explain: The clause has no verb. The pronoun between 'you' and 'the head' marks the join. Do not read it as a second 'he'.

practice.prompt: What does אִיתַי (word 0) do in אִיתַי גְּבַר בְּמַלְכוּתָךְ?

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: there is a man in thy kingdom, in whom is the spirit of the holy gods; and in the days of thy father light and understanding and wisdom, like the wisdom of the gods, was found in him; and the king Nebuchadnezzar thy father, the king, I say, thy father, made him master of the magicians, enchanters, Chaldeans, and astrologers;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It says that something exists: 'there is'
practice.explain: אִיתַי introduces what exists, here a man in the kingdom. It does not take a subject before it; the thing that exists follows.

practice.prompt: How is the clause חָכְמְתָא וּגְבוּרְתָא דִּי לֵהּ הִיא (words 13 to 17) built?

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Daniel spoke and said: Blessed be the name of God from everlasting even unto everlasting; for wisdom and might are His;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A verbless clause: 'wisdom and might' are the subject, 'his' is the predicate, and הִיא links them
A verbal clause with the verb הִיא
A question with לֵהּ as the subject
practice.explain: Two nouns, then לֵהּ, 'to him', then the linking pronoun. English adds 'are'; Aramaic does not need it.

check.prompt: Which word is the subject of שָׂמְתָּ, 'you set' (word 2)?

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: Thou, O king, hast made a decree, that every man that shall hear the sound of the horn, pipe, harp, trigon, psaltery, and bagpipe, and all kinds of music, shall fall down and worship the golden image;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

check.explain: The ending of שָׂמְתָּ already says 'you'. The pronoun אַנְתְּ, which stands first, repeats it for emphasis and addresses the king. טְּעֵם, 'decree', is the object.

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: All the presidents of the kingdom, the prefects and the satraps, the ministers and the governors, have consulted together that the king should establish a statute, and make a strong interdict, that whosoever shall ask a petition of any god or man for thirty days, save of thee, O king, he shall be cast into the den of lions.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: With a clause that has no verb
With the subject, and the verb comes at the end
With the verb אִתְיָעַטוּ, and its subject, 'all the officials of the kingdom', follows
With the object of the verb
check.explain: The verb stands first and the subject (כֹּל סָרְכֵי מַלְכוּתָא and the others in the list) follows it. Aramaic has verb-first clauses beside verb-late ones.

check.prompt: Which word is the main verb of the clause whose subject is תַּתְּנַי, Tattenai (word 1)?

quoted.title: Ezra
quoted.english: Then Tattenai, the governor beyond the River, Shethar-bozenai, and their companions, because that Darius the king had thus sent, acted with all diligence.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

check.explain: שְׁלַח belongs to the clause about Darius (its subject is דָּרְיָוֶשׁ מַלְכָּא). The plural verb עֲבַדוּ, 'they did', at the end of the sentence matches Tattenai and his colleagues.

check.prompt: Which word is the object of כְּתַבוּ, 'they wrote' (word 5)?

quoted.title: Ezra
quoted.english: Rehum the commander and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes the king in this sort —
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

check.explain: אִגְּרָה חֲדָה, 'one letter', is what they wrote. סָפְרָא, 'the scribe', is part of the subject; the other two words follow prepositions.

check.prompt: Which word is the object of פָלְחִין, 'serving' (word 23)?

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: There are certain Jews whom thou hast appointed over the affairs of the province of Babylon, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego; these men, O king, have not regarded thee: they serve not thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

check.explain: The object stands before the negative and the participle, and its לְ marks it: 'your god they do not serve'. מַלְכָּא is the king being addressed.

check.prompt: Which is the subject of אֱלָהֲכוֹן הוּא אֱלָהּ אֱלָהִין (words 7 to 10)?

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: The king spoke unto Daniel, and said: 'Of a truth it is, that your God is the God of gods, and the Lord of kings, and a revealer of secrets, seeing thou hast been able to reveal this secret.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

check.explain: There is no verb. 'Your God' is what is spoken about, הוּא links, and 'God of gods' says what he is.

check.prompt: How does the clause say that 'no hurt is in them' (words 11 to 14)?

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: He answered and said: 'Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt; and the appearance of the fourth is like a son of the gods.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: With אִיתַי, negated by לָא, and a phrase with בְּ
With a perfect verb and the object marker לְ
check.explain: חֲבָל, 'hurt', is the subject; לָא אִיתַי says 'there is not'; בְּהוֹן says where. English says 'they have no hurt'; Aramaic says 'hurt is not in them'.

check.prompt: How is the idea 'and it had four wings' built in וְלַהּ גַּפִּין אַרְבַּע (words 7 to 9)?

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: After this I beheld, and lo another, like a leopard, which had upon the sides of it four wings of a fowl; the beast had also four heads; and dominion was given to it.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: אַרְבַּע is the subject and גַּפִּין the predicate, joined by הוּא
לַהּ names the owner, 'to it', and the clause has no verb
לַהּ is the object of a verb of seeing
check.explain: Ownership is shown by לְ with a suffix: 'to it (were) four wings'. The animals were seen by the narrator, but לַהּ does not depend on that verb.

check.prompt: In what order are the parts of בֵּהּ בְּלֵילְיָא קְטִיל בֵּלְאשַׁצַּר מַלְכָּא כַשְׂדָּאָה?

quoted.title: Daniel
quoted.english: In that night Belshazzar the Chaldean king was slain.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

check.explain: בֵּהּ בְּלֵילְיָא, 'in that night', is a phrase of time; קְטִיל, 'was killed', is the verb; Belshazzar the king is the subject. The verb comes before its subject here.

reading.why: The Chaldeans accuse the three Jews and they answer the king. These verses have fronted objects (לֵאלָהָךְ לָא פָלְחִין), אִיתַי with and without a suffix, verbs placed late, and nominal clauses, so you can practise finding subject, verb and object in each.

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: There are certain Jews whom thou hast appointed over the affairs of the province of Babylon, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego; these men, O king, have not regarded thee: they serve not thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.'
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: Then Nebuchadnezzar in his rage and fury commanded to bring Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego. Then were these men brought before the king.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: Nebuchadnezzar spoke and said unto them: 'Is it true, O Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego, that ye serve not my gods, nor worship the golden image which I have set up?
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: Now if ye be ready that at what time ye hear the sound of the horn, pipe, harp, trigon, psaltery, and bagpipe, and all kinds of music, ye fall down and worship the image which I have made, well; but if ye worship not, ye shall be cast the same hour into the midst of a burning fiery furnace; and who is the god that shall deliver you out of my hands?'
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego, answered and said to the king: 'O Nebuchadnezzar, we have no need to answer thee in this matter.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: If our God whom we serve is able to deliver us, He will deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and out of thy hand, O king.
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

segments.title: Daniel
segments.english: But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.'
segments.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

Every Aramaic word shown as an example, in a paradigm or in an exercise is taken from the Aramaic of the Westminster Leningrad Codex as analysed by the Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible project.
